explanation: Assumption: The default by-value capture clause (`[=]`) guarantees that the resulting lambda is self-contained and isolated from external state changes. Reality: `[=]` only captures non-static local variables by value. Static variables, global variables, and static member variables used within the lambda are accessed by name lookup (effectively by reference) and are *not* copied into the closure. Why It Fails: If the external static state changes after the lambda is created, the lambda's behavior changes unexpectedly, directly contradicting the perceived isolation of the by-value capture mechanism. This failure leads to hidden dependencies on mutable shared state.
practical_example: A developer uses `[=]` inside a factory function that returns a lambda meant to be stored in a collection. If the lambda relies on a static counter or configuration variable that changes over time, all previously stored lambdas will exhibit the new behavior, causing difficult-to-trace bugs related to temporal coupling.
keywords: Lambda capture static variables, Lambda capture global variables, C++ lambda capture rules
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
